sec.title: Background
sec.p: Plant compactness (PC) is a crucial agronomic trait that affects plant density in wheat, which in turn influences biomass and grain yield potential. The canopy of high-yielding wheat varieties should exhibit appropriate aboveground plant architecture. In this study, three recombinant inbred line (RIL) populations were generated to identify and validate quantitative trait loci (QTL) related to plant compactness. The erect and compact tillering genotype SN05525 was used as a common parent. A total of 193 F8 RILs from the cross SN05525/SN22 were genotyped using the high-density Illumina iSelect 90 K single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) assay.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A linkage map with 7180 SNP loci was constructed, revealing six QTL on chromosomes 3B (Qpc.sdau-3B.1, Qpc.sdau-3B.2),5B (Qpc.sdau-5B), 5D (Qpc.sdau-5D), 2 A (Qpc.sdau-2 A), and 7 A (Qpc.sdau-7 A) that control compact tillers. Qpc.sdau-3B.1, Qpc.sdau-5D, and Qpc.sdau-5B accounted for up to 16.70%, 16.89%, and 14.56% of the phenotypic variance, respectively. Kompetitive allele-specific PCR (KASP) markers were developed for these QTL, and their effects were validated in two additional RIL populations, SN05525/Luyuan 502 and SN05525/Xinong 511. Significant effects of Qpc.sdau-3B.1 and Qpc.sdau-5D on compactness were observed in the validation populations.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Three major QTL loci closely related to plant compactness in wheat were successfully identified, and their effects were validated in two additional RIL populations across multi environments. Plant architecture plays a crucial role in enhancing yield and economic value in wheat. In the process of molecular marker-assisted selection breeding, the closely linked KASP markers could potentially be utilized in molecular marker-assisted selection for adjusting plant compactness and for further characterization of the underlying gene(s).

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Common wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) ranks as the second most extensively cultivated crop globally, playing a crucial role in ensuring global food security [1]. Cultivated across over 220 million hectares worldwide, this crop fulfills approximately 20% of the world’s daily caloric and protein needs [2]. An improvement in the yield potential of wheat is important to satisfy the escalating nutritional needs of the expanding global populace [2, 3]. Morphological characteristics of common wheat play a special role in increasing yield, and many physiologists and breeders would like to identify specific characteristics that could successfully be incorporated into commercial varieties in breeding programs [4]. Donald coined the term “ideotype” to describe those morphological characteristics in a wheat crop that would theoretically result in the highest yields given adequate soil fertility and water availability [5].

The plant architecture in wheat includes plant height, tiller number, and tiller spacing. An ideal plant architecture should allow for efficient light transmission, proper ventilation, and improved photosynthetic efficiency, lodging and drought resistance, and water retention throughout the growth stages of wheat [6, 7]. Understanding the genetic mechanisms underlying plant architecture is crucial for molecular marker-assisted selection and molecular breeding in wheat. This understanding involves identifying QTL closely linked to specific traits in breeding lines or germplasm resources, as well as pinpointing candidate genes through fine mapping to validate their biological functions using genetic methodologies [8, 9].

Plant height (PH) is a crucial trait related to plant architecture and yield potential in wheat [10]. There is plenty of available literature on QTL mapping and exploring the genetic mechanisms of plant height. Over the past two decades, the successful application of quantitative-genetic methodology has facilitated the identification of 167 QTL for PH in wheat, which are distributed on almost all chromosomes [11–13].

As shorter stature reduces the incidence of lodging, particularly when plants are grown under high fertilizer regimes [14], more research and utilization focused on QTL related to plant dwarfing. To date, 25 reduced height genes (Rht1-Rht25) have been identified in wheat [12, 15]. Rht-B1/Rht-D1, located on chromosomes 4B and 4D, respectively, have been characterized at biological and molecular levels [16]. Peng proved that Rht-B1/Rht-D1, the orthologues of the Arabidopsis Gibberellin Insensitive (GAI) gene, encode DELLA proteins, which act to repress gibberellic acid (GA)-responsive growth, and their mutant alleles Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b confer dwarfism by producing more active forms of these growth repressors [17]. Since the 1960s, Rht-B1b or Rht-D1bhave been introduced into wheat varieties via crosses with semi-dwarf wheat, making major contributions to global wheat production since the 1960s [18]. Pearce showed that the semi-dwarfing alleles Rht-B1d and Rht-B1e introduce premature stop codons within the amino-terminal coding region. These newly characterized mutations in Rht-B1 and Rht-D1 confer “GA-insensitive” dwarfism by producing DELLA proteins that do not bind the GA receptor GA INSENSITIVE DWARF1, potentially compromising their targeted degradation [19].

The other extensively used dwarfing gene in wheat breeding is Rht8, and both its height-increasing and dwarfing alleles are responsive to GA (GA-sensitive) [15, 20].The semi-dwarfing gene Rht8 effectively supplements the deficiencies of Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b, leading to its extensive incorporation into wheat cultivars worldwide following its transfer from the Japanese strain Akakomugi to European wheat during the 1930s [7, 21].The microsatellite marker Xgwm261 has been widely used for identifying Rht8 in global wheat germplasm [22–25]. The semi-dwarf characteristic induced by Rht8 is correlated with decreased responsiveness to brassinosteroid hormone. Furthermore, novel gene-derived markers, which exhibit a closer linkage to Rht8 compared to Xgwm261, have been generated [26]. Rht8 encodes a protein containing a zinc finger BED-type motif and an RNase H-like domain that regulates plant height via influencing bioactive GA biosynthesis. Modern wheat breeding has extensively utilized Rht8 itself, or stacked it together with other Rht loci to maximize lodging resistance and yield [20].

Tillering is a crucial agronomic trait which shapes grain yield and tiller number (TN) is a remarkable factor in the formation of aboveground plant architecture in wheat. Many TN-related QTL with major phenotypic effects were documented utilizing different mapping populations in common wheat. Productive tiller number (PTN) or effective tiller number, defined as the number of tillers that produce spikes and seeds per unit area, is a key component of grain yield in wheat. At present, many researchers have detected major QTL for PTN independently on chromosome 4 A, 6 A, 1B, 4B and 6B, and the explained phenotypic variation ranged from 9.6 to 45.46% in different studies [27–30]. In winter wheat, pre-winter tillers are more inclined to form spikes than spring tillers. Li reported that a total of 27 significant QTL related to tillering, including maximum tillering before winter (MTW), maximum tillering in spring (MTS), and effective tillering at harvest (ETH), were detected across environments in two populations [31]. By genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis, Bilgrami identified a total of 47 significant marker-trait associations (MTAs) for total tiller number (TTN) and fertile tiller number (FTN) in Iranian bread wheat under different water regimes [32]. Spike formation rate (SR), which is based on maximum tiller number and spike number per unit area, is a tillering related trait in wheat. A stable and major QTL (QMTN.sicau-4D) for spike formation rate was localized to chromosome 4D and explained 18.24–24.48% of the observed phenotypic variance, and it might be novel pleiotropic QTL, which also controlled maximum tiller number per unit area (MTN) and tiller number during pre-winter per unit area (QTNW.sicau-4D)(Hu et al., 2017) [1, 33]. Dynamic QTL analyses provide a better understanding of the QTL controlling the tiller number at different growth stages. A total of 28 single-environment QTL were identified in RIL populations at four growth stages, and among these, seven QTL were stable and used for multi-environment and dynamic analysis. These QTL were mapped to chromosome 4 A, 5 A, 2D, 4D, 5D, and 7D. Each QTL explained 1.63–21.22% of the observed phenotypic variation, with an additive effect from − 20.51 to 11.59 [34]. In investigations centered on quantitative trait loci (QTL) associated with the enhancement of tiller numbers, three QTL governing decreased tillering were also detected on the chromosome 5 A, 2B, and 2D [35]. Several studies have been conducted on TN-related genes in common wheat, focusing on their genetic and physiological mechanisms. One such gene, TaD27-B, is considered an ortholog of rice D27 and is responsible for encoding an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of strigolactones (SLs). The roles of SLs in regulating bud outgrowth have been extensively described in various model plant species [28, 36]. Zhao proved that TaD27-RNAi wheat plants had more tillers, and TaD27-B-OE wheat plants had fewer tillers implying TaD27-B is a key factor in the regulation of tiller number in wheat [37]. The role of OTUB1 in regulating tiller numbers in rice has been reported [38] and TaOTUB1s were identified and proved to influence tiller number in wheat [39].

In addition to plant height and tiller number, the plant architecture could also be represented by tiller angles in a whole plant, which is an important factor determining plant’s aboveground shape in wheat. Plant compactness is an indicator to describe the convergence degree of wheat tillers in the fields [7] and it could be roughly divided into loose or tight types according to the spatial distribution of tillers in wheat practice [6]. However, compared with the significant progress in plant height and tiller number, there is relatively little research reported on compactness in common wheat. Zhao reported that two QTL on chromosomes 1AL and 5DL were identified with reduced tiller angle, and the major stable QTL, QTA.caas-5DL, was detected across all experimental conditions, explaining 13.8–24.8% of the variability in phenotypic traits [40].

In present study, three recombinant inbred line (RIL) populations were developed between varieties with significant differences in the plant shape aboveground, assessed for plant compactness in field environments, and analyzed for genetic variations using SNP markers. The aims of the current investigation encompassed: (1) the delineation of genetic loci governing plant compactness in the RIL populations through QTL mapping, and (2) the verification of the impacts of the identified QTL, alongside the creation of user-friendly markers for molecular marker-assisted selection (MAS).

sec.title: Experimental materials and plant cultivation
sec.p: Three RIL populations were generated and used in this study, and Shannong 05525 (SN05525), a compact plant genotype with upward tillers, was used as a common parent (Fig. 1). A total of 193 RILs (F8:9) used for QTL mapping were developed from Shannong 22 (SN22) and SN05525, designated as SS population. SN22, a high-yielding wheat cultivar planted mainly in Huanghuai wheat zone in China, has strong tillering ability and loose plant type (Fig. 1). SN22 was examined and approved as a cultivar by Variety Examination and Approval Committee in Shandong Province in 2011. The second RIL population (SN05525/Luyuan502, SL) consisted of 136 F7 lines, while the third RIL (SN05525/Xinong511, SX) consisted of 112 F6 lines. Similar to SN22, both Luyuan502and Xinong511 exhibit a loose plant type. The latter two populations were used to validate the effects of putative QTL identified in the mapping population. These populations were generated by single seed descent in the field in Taian City in Shandong Province, China (36°09′N, 117°09′E, and elevation 493.3 m above sea level).

sec.p: Phenotypic evaluation of all populations for plant architecture was conducted in the fields for all populations during the wheat growing seasons. Each line in a population was planted with 5 rows spaced 25 cm apart. Thirty and twenty seeds per 2 m row were manually planted individually using SS population in Taian and Zaozhuang in 2017–2018 (designated as TA2018-1, TA2018-2; ZZ2018-1, ZZ2018-2). In the following growing seasons, twenty seeds per 2 m row were applied in experiments using SS population in Taian (TA2019), Zaozhuang (ZZ2019), Xiajin (XJ2019), Weifang (WF2019) and Jining (JN2019) in 2018–2019. Twenty seeds per 2 m row were applied in experiments using SL and SX populations in Taian and Zaozhuang in 2018–2019 and 2019–2020. All the field experiments were managed according to the same methods employed locally for wheat production. In total, SS population with 9 environments (combinations of the growth season, location and plant density) was used for QTL mapping and two populations (SL and SX) were used for QTL validation.

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation
sec.p: The architecture of wheat plants in all populations was assessed 10 days after heading. Plant compactness (PC) can be measured as the maximum distance between tillers (MDBT in cm), which can be determined at 30 cm above ground level using a measuring ruler on a single plant. More than three plants in each row from the second to fourth rows were selected for measuring the MDBT. The mean in each row was calculated and used in the analysis. The frequency distribution of MDBT in each environment and their correlation were analyzed using SPSS version 20.0 for Windows (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Broad-sense heritability (h2) was calculated across environments as described by Smithh2 was calculated from σG2∕σP2, where σG2represents the genetic variance, and σP2represents the phenotypic variance. The other agronomic and morphological traits (such as plant height, anthesis day, tiller number, 1000 grain weight, etc.) in SL and SX populations were investigated according to conventional procedures [41]. The best linear unbiased predictions (BLUPs) for each agronomic trait across various testing environments were computed utilizing the MIXED procedure in R software, version 3.5.2 [42]. The 3σ criterion was subsequently applied to identify and exclude extreme values that significantly diverged from the population mean. This methodology, with fixed effects encompassing the overall mean and random effects accounting for genetic variations among genotypes and environmental influences, was utilized for an estimation of genotypic performance even in the presence of environmental variability. The correlations between the investigated traits were calculated based on the BLUP values, and Student’s t-test was performed to determine significant differences using SPSS 20.0.

sec.title: Molecular genotyping and linkage map construction
sec.p: Molecular genotyping and linkage map construction were conducted by extracting genomic DNA from 30-day-old seedlings of the parents and recombinant inbred lines (RILs) from three populations utilizing the Cetyltrime-thylammonium Bromide (CTAB) method [43]. DNA concentration was measured using a Thermo Scientific NanoDrop 2000. The DNA samples of the 193 RILs and parents from the mapping population SS were genotyped using the 90 K wheat Infinium iSelect SNP arrays developed by Illumina Inc [44]. The SNP assays were performed at the Genomics & Bioinformatics Services of the Agriculture Research Center at the University of Illinois, Illinois according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). Normalized Cy3 and Cy5 fluorescence intensities for each DNA sample were graphed using GenomeStudio software (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA), resulting in genotype clustering for each SNP marker.

SNPs with more than 10% missing data were removed, and biallelic polymorphic loci were selected for the next Linkage map construction. The linkage maps were constructed using the MAP function in IciMapping 4.1 [45], and the parameters for the linkage map construction were set as follows: “nnTwoOpt” for algorithm, “SARF” for criterion, and “5” for window size. LOD thresholds between 1.5 and 3.0 were tested until a threshold with the optimum number of markers in linkage groups was obtained, maintaining linkage order and distance.

sec.title: QTL detection
sec.p: Phenotypic data obtained from individual environments and the integrated analysis (BLUP) across nine environments were utilized for the detection of QTL. QTL analysis was performed by inclusive composite interval mapping (ICIM) using the additive module of IciMapping 4.1. Kruskal–Wallis test was used to evaluate the degree of association between markers and MDBTs. For each environment, a test of 1000 permutations was performed to identify the logarithm of odds (LOD) threshold corresponding to a genome-wide false discovery rate of 1%. Based on the permutation test, threshold LOD values between 2.5 and 3.5 were used to confirm the presence of a QTL. To characterize the physical positions of the identified QTL, QTL-associated SNP marker sequences were aligned to the Chinese Spring wheat Reference Sequence (CS RefSeq v1.0) released by the International Wheat Genome Sequence Consortium (IWGSC) through a BLAST search (http://wheat-urgi.versailles.inra.fr/).

sec.title: KASP assays and QTL validation using two populations
sec.p: The SN05525/Luyuan502 (SL) RIL and SN05525/Xinong511 (SX) RIL (i.e., SL and SX populations) were used to validate the genetic effects of the major QTL in different genetic backgrounds. For the QTL on chromosomes 3B, 5D and 5B, QTL-associated SNP markers were selected respectively and converted into Kompetitive allele specific PCR (KASP) markers using PolyMarker [46].

The KASP markers identified in this study served as either the highest point or the neighboring markers for every discerned QTL across the chromosomes. Only those KASP markers demonstrating consistent segregation patterns with the respective SNP markers in both parents and the mapping population were employed to screen the two validation populations. KASP chain reaction primers were designed and are listed in Table S1.

KASP assays were performed in a CFX96 Touch™ real-time PCR detection system and the fluorescence signals of the samples were recorded and analyzed using the genotyping module of BioRad CFX manager (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA). The reaction system and PCR conditions were based on the protocol from LGC Genomics (https://shop.lgcgenomics.com/).

Homozygous RILs were identified and selected based on a combination of KASP marker alleles for a specific QTL in the respective validation populations, and were divided into the following two groups based on the genotyping results: lines with homozygous alleles from SN05525 (designated as AA) and lines with homozygous alleles from the other parents (designated as BB). The differences in MDBT between the two groups in the populations were evaluated using Student’s t-test (P < 0.05).

sec.title: Plant compactness of the SN05525/SN22 population
sec.p: In the different growth environments, the MDBTs at 30 cm above ground of SN05525 ranged from 13.1 to 18.9 cm, and those of SN22 ranged from 22.8 to 32.6 cm. The mean of MDBTs in SN22 was 80.2% more (P < 0.01) than that of SN05525. SN05525 exhibited significantly higher compactness than SN22 in all environments (Table 1). MDBTs in the SN05525/SN22 population displayed a continuous distribution, ranging from 10.3 to 34.9 cm, with the transgressive segregations observed in each growth environment within the populations (Fig. S1). This implies that plant compactness in wheat is affected by multiple loci, and there is significant genetic variation for MDBT in the population across all environments. The PC showed high broad-sense heritability (0.735) based on nine environments in 2 years and the BLUP value (Table 1). Correlation coefficients (r) of MDBTs between different environments were all significant, ranging from 0.467 to 0.823 (P < 0.05) (Table 2).

sec.title: Linkage map constructed from the SN05525/SN22 RIL population
sec.p: Among 81,587 SNPs used in screening the SN05525/SN22 population, 9018 SNP markers (11.05%) were polymorphic between the two parental lines. Of those, 124 markers had more than 10% missing data points in the RILs, and 1770 were not anchored on the linkage map.

In total, 7180 SNP markers were used for constructing a linkage map that consisted of twenty-one linkage groups corresponding to the 21 hexaploid wheat chromosomes, covering a total genetic distance of 3656 cM with an average interval distance of 0.51 cM (Table S2). 3103 markers (43.5%) were localized to the A genome, spanning a total genetic length of 1684.7 cM with an average marker density of 0.54 cM. In contrast, 3557 markers (49.9%) were mapped to the B genome, covering a total genetic distance of 1420.5 cM with an average marker density of 0.40 cM. Additionally, 464 markers (6.51%) were assigned to the D genome, spanning a total genetic length of 550.8 cM with an average marker density of 1.19 cM (Table S3). The genetic map displayed an average chromosome length of 174.1 cM, ranging from 18.1 cM (6D) to 301.9 cM (3 A). The number of SNP markers varied across wheat chromosomes, with a range from 42 on chromosome 2D to 628 on chromosome 2B. While SNP markers were evenly distributed across the genome, chromosomes 1D, 3D, 4D, 5D, and 6D exhibited lower marker densities. The overall SNP density averaged 1.94 SNP/cM, with the highest density observed on chromosome 6B at 3.90 SNP and the lowest on chromosome 2D at 0.4 SNP.

sec.title: Identification of QTL controlling plant compactness in the SN05525/SN22 RIL population
sec.p: The study identified QTL responsible for controlling plant compactness within the SN05525/SN22RIL population. Using MDBTs collected from 9 distinct environments and the BLUP dataset (Table 3), QTL associated with plant compactness were pinpointed. Permutation tests established LOD values falling between 2.5 and 3.5 as thresholds for these environments. Through ICIM analysis, six QTL governing plant compactness were identified within the SN05525/SN22 population, located on chromosomes 2 A, 7 A, 3B (2 QTL), 5B, and 5D (Table 3). All alleles responsible for the compact plant architecture trait were all contributed by SN05525.

caption.p: Quantitative trait locus for plant compactness (PC) identified in SN05525/SN22 population from different environments and BLUP dataset

sec.p: The first two plant compactness QTL were Qpc.sdau-3B.1 and Qpc.sdau-5D. The “pc” and “sdau” in the QTL names denote “plant compactness” and “Shandong Agriculture University”. Qpc.sdau-3B.1 was located on the long arm of Chr.3B (Fig. 2) and the flanking SNP markers were Excalibur_c16569_765 andBS00022582_51. Qpe.sdau-5D was located on the long arm of Chr. 5D (Fig. 2) and the flanking SNP markers were GENE-3232_217 and RAC875_c53407_97. Both QTL had a stable expression across the 9 environments, and explained 9.86–21.6% and 8.2–16.7% of the phenotypic variance, respectively (Table 3). The two QTL could be designated as major and stable loci for controlling PC.

caption.p: Linkage maps and locations of wheat plant compactness associated QTL (Qpcsdau-3B.1, Qpc-sdau-3B.2 and Qpc-sdau-5D, black bars) identified in chromosome 3B (left) and 5D (right) in the RIL population SN05525/SN22

sec.p: The third QTL (Qpc.sdau-5B) was located on the long arm of Chr. 5B (Fig. 3) and the flanking SNP markers were CAP12_c7929_116 and GENE-3310_792. Qpc.sdau-5B was specifically detected in six environments except ZZ2018-2, TA2019 and ZZ2019, and explained 4.39–7.65% of the phenotypic variance (Table 3).

caption.p: Linkage maps and locations of wheat plant compactness associated QTL (Qpcsdau-5B and Qpc-sdau-2 A, black bars) identified in chromosome 5B (left) and 2 A (right) in the RIL population SN05525/SN22

sec.p: The forth locus (Qpc.sdau-2 A) were located on the long arm of Chr. 2 A, and the flanking SNP markers were Tdurum_contig15156_730 and Kukri_rep_c105874_631 (Fig. 3). Qpc.sdau-4D was specifically detected in four environments, excluding TA2018-1, ZZ2018-1, TA2019, XJ2019 and JN2019. It explained 3.56–7.63% of the phenotypic variance (Table 3).

The fifth QTL (Qpc.sdau-7 A) was located on the long arm of Chr. 7 A, and the flanking SNP markers were Excalibur_c780_400 and Tdurum_contig42638_383 (Fig. 4). Qpc.sdau-7 A was specifically detected in TA2018-1, ZZ2018-1, ZZ2019 and WF2019, and accounted for 3.67–6.21% of the phenotypic variance (Table 3).

caption.p: Linkage map and location of wheat plant compactness associated QTL (Qpcsdau-7 A, black bar) identified in chromosome 7 A in the RIL population SN05525/SN22

sec.p: The sixth QTL (Qpc.sdau-3B.2) was located on the short arm of Chr. 3B, and the flanking SNP markers were BS00066108_51 and wsnp_BE498786B_Ta_2_1 (Fig. 2). Qpc.sdau-3B.2 was specifically detected in TA2018-1, ZZ2018-1 and XJ2019, and accounted for 3.67–6.21% of the phenotypic variance (Table 3).

Based on the published data from the IWGSC, Qpc. sdau-3B.1 was about mapped between 817.8 and 826 Mb on Chr.3BL; Qpc.sdau-5D was mapped between 403.6 and 413.9 Mb on Chr. 5DL; and Qpc.sdau-5B was mapped between 488.5 and 501.3 Mb on Chr. 5BL.

sec.title: Effects of compacting QTL in different genetic backgrounds
sec.p: The effects of the three QTL, Qpc.sdau-3B.1, Qpc.sdau-5D, and Qpc.sdau-5B, on plant compactness were evaluated by Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP). QTL-associated SNP markers were converted to KASP markers. Five primer pairs were designed, and two populations with different genetic backgrounds were used.

The markers KASP-BS00109691_51 and KASP-BobWhite_s64174_14 were used to evaluate the effects of Qpc.sdau-3B.1 in the SL and SX populations. A total of 72 and 83 homozygous genotypes were in the SL and SX populations respectively. The participants were divided into two groups (AA or BB) (Table 4). Significant differences (P < 0.01) were detected between the two groups in each population. The MDBTs differed between the two groups by 14.2–15.4% and 6.7–7.9% in the SL and SX populations, respectively (Table 4).

sec.p: For Qpc.sdau-5D, the KASP-D_contig78682_498 marker and corresponding homozygous genotypes in the SL and SX populations were used. The average MDBTs in homozygous “AA” genotypes ranged from 12.4 to 16.3 and were significantly lower (P < 0.01) than those in homozygous “BB” genotypes with the range from 15.2 to 19.3 (Table 4). The effects ranged from 13.2 to 18.4% with an average of 15.5% in both populations (Table 4).

For Qltn.sicau-5B, the KASP-Excalibur_c96334_93 and KASP- RAC875_c13478_332 were used to evaluate the effects of allele pairs in the SL and SX populations, respectively. The average compactness of the plant was significantly different between the two groups in the SL population in the two validation environments. However, there were no significant differences in the SX population (Table 4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: China is one of the most important wheat producing countries in the world. Huanghuai wheat zone is the main wheat production area in China. The planting area and output in this area account for about 45% and 48% of the national field area and total output respectively [47, 48]. Wheat variety Bainong sterility (BNS) is a photosensitive and thermosensitive genetic male sterile line, and has complete sterility, stable genetic performance and suitability for planting in Huanghuai wheat zone [49–53]. SN05525 is the only excellent restoration line suitable for growing in Huanghuai wheat zone [49, 51, 53], and it possesses compact plant architecture with high yield, lodging and disease resistances. In the process of selecting new restoration lines from SN05525 offspring, multiple genetic populations were constructed in our laboratory and utilized in this study.

In a previous study, two quantitative trait loci (QTL) on chromosomes 1AL and 5DL were identified with low tiller angle alleles contributed by Zhongmai895, which explained 5.4–11.2% and 13.8–24.8% of the phenotypic variances [40]. In this study, QTL controlling plant compactness was identified in the SN05525/SN22 RIL population. These QTL were located on chromosomes 2 A, 7 A, 3B (2 QTL), 5B, and 5D (Table 3; Figs. 2, 3 and 4) and explained 2.69–21.6% of the phenotypic variances.

Qpc.sdau-3B.1, as a major stable QTL, was located in a 6.47 cM region on chromosome 3B, flanked by markers Excalibur_c16569_765 and BS00068415_51, spanning from 817.8 to 826.0 Mb according to Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC, https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast_iwgsc/). This QTL explains 9.86–21.6% of the phenotypic variances in all the trial environments. The region surrounding Qpc.sdau-3B.1 on chromosome 3B is rich in grain characteristic-related QTL, such as QTkw.cau-3B.1 (thousand-kernel weight), QKwpp-3B.1 (kernel weight per spike), QKnps-3B.1 (kernel number per spike), QKnps-3B.2, and QKL-3B.1 (kernel length) etc [54, 55]. Among these QTL, QTgw.cau-3B.1 was a major stable QTL that accounted for > 10% of the phenotypic variation. It was located from 698.62 to 760.71 Mb according to Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC, https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast _iwgsc /) [55].

Zanke reported that in eight environments, a natural population with a panel of 358 European winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) varieties and 14 spring wheat varieties found the most TKW enhancing (“best”) alleles were found near Tdurum_contig59953_220, approximately 772.3 MB according to the Chinese Spring reference genome [56].

A marker-trait association (MTA) for early season nitrogen (ESN) was identified on chromosome 3B in a genome-wide association study using 105 elite wheat varieties (lines). The MTA was near Excalibur_c15944_70, approximately 799 Mb according to Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC,https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast_iwgsc/, v1.0) [38]. This suggests that there may be multiple QTL loci responsible for regulating yield and morphological traits in this specific area. Qpc.sdau-3B.1 may be a QTL with pleiotropic effects or tightly linked to these QTL controlling grain characteristics, and it would be beneficial to clarify the relationship among QTL in this area for molecular marker-assisted breeding in the future. In addition, more than 160 annotated genes have been found in this region by gene query according to Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC, https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast_iwgsc/). As a major stable QTL controlling PC, Qpc.sdau-3B.1 could be utilized in a breeding program to achieve an optimal plant architecture in wheat. To obtain the information on the function or molecular mechanism, it is necessary to construct a higher density linkage map in this region and to obtain the QTL with a much higher resolution position.

Qpc.sdau-5D is another detected major stable QTL for plant compactness that has been detected in all the nine test environments. It was located in a 4.68 cM region, flanked by markers GENE-3232_217 and RAC875_c53407_97, spanning from 403.0 to 413.5 Mb according to Chinese Spring reference genome (IWGSC, https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast_iwgsc/), and explains 8.2–16.7% of the phenotypic variances in these environments. Zhao identified a QTL for low tiller angle that was located at 408.6 and 418.4 Mb on chromosome 5D, which overlaps with the region identified in our study [40]. They proposed TraesCS5D02G322600 as a candidate gene in their identified region for reducing tiller angle, and designated it as TaTAC-D1. Initially, it was also proven that TaTAC-D1 might be the causal gene for the reduction in tiller angle by detecting the phenotypic differences of various alleles in validation populations. In sequence alignment, TaTAC-D1appeared to be a putative TILLER ANGLE CONTROL 1 (TAC1) ortholog in wheat. TAC1, an IGT gene family member, is an important regulator of lateral organ orientation, and its orthologs have been found and identified in many species [57]. OsTAC1 plays a critical role in controlling rice plant architecture. High expression of OsTAC1 results in wider tiller angle and more tillers, while low expression leads to erect tillers with a smaller tiller angle [58]. ZmTAC1 controlled the size of the leaf angle and its expression was the highest in the leaf-sheath pulvinus. A nucleotide difference in the 5’-untranslated region (UTR) between the compact inbred line and the expanded inbred line influences the expression level of ZmTAC1 [59].

Alteration of TAC1 expression in Prunus species leads to pleiotropic shoot phenotypes. In particular, severely vertical branches are observed in PpeTAC1 overexpression in Prunus persica, which are oriented similarly to those in pillar peaches but with an even narrower profile. In contrast, PpeTAC1 overexpression in plum led to trees with wider branch angles and more horizontal branch orientations. In addition, pillar peach trees and transgenic plum lines exhibited pleiotropic phenotypes, including differences in trunk and branch diameter, stem growth, and twisting branch phenotypes [57].

All these results implied that lateral branches, tillers, leaves, and flower buds of plants with loss-of-function tac1 mutations or reduced TAC1 expression exhibit upright orientations. Those findings demonstrate that TAC1 promotes horizontal lateral organ orientations. The plant architecture controlling function and corresponding molecular basis of TaTAC-D1 in wheat need to be verified by genetic methods, and the pleiotropic effect of TaTAC-D1 needs to be characterized. All of this information has certain guiding significance for pyramiding breeding in the future.

Besides Qpc-sdau-3B.1 and Qpc-sdau-5D, four QTL for PC identified in this study based on MDBT, located at chromosome 5B, 2 A, 7 A and 3B, were not detected at all test environments, and they explained 4.39–7.65%, 3.56–7.63%, 3.67–6.21% and 2.69–3.59% of the phenotypic variance, respectively. The weaker effects of the four QTL on plant compactness might classify them as minor QTL.

The existence of minor QTL could result from the fact that the traits are not only governed by additive gene effects but also significantly influenced by the complex gene interactions, including dominance, epistatic and genotype × environment interaction component effects [60, 61].

Generally, it is believed that the minor QTL would be difficult to retain in a breeding program when present singly, and would be easily masked in the presence of more effective genes. Although the effects of these minor QTL/genes are relatively low, sometimes they might be of great significance in crop breeding practice [62–64].

At present, many minor effect disease resistance QTL of wheat have been identified and utilized in disease resistance breeding [65, 66]. Breeding for quantitative resistance conferred by minor-effect genes tends to result in more durable resistance in breeding lines, but it requires multiple breeding cycles to gradually enhance resistance [67].

It is believed that the methodology used for quantitative resistance is similar to the breeding method for other complex traits such as grain yield(González-Camacho et al., 2018; Poland and Rutkoski, 2016; Rutkoski et al., 2014) [2–4, 67–69]. It is worth trying to utilize the compactness QTL with minor effects detected in this study in future plant architecture breeding.

The grain yield in wheat, which could be estimated by the effective tiller number (ETN), grain number per spike (GNS), and thousand kernel weight (TKW), and is profoundly influenced by anthesis date (AD) and plant height (PH), among other factors. It is necessary to analyze the correlations between these agronomic traits and MDBT in different environments within specific populations.

The MDBT was highly positively correlated with the effective tiller number (P < 0.01). Moreover, there were significant differences in the MDBT between the two groups (lines with or without positive alleles of Qpc-sdau-3B.1 in the RILs and 2 validation populations) (Table S4).

However, the MDBT was negatively correlated with the GN (P < 0.05) and there were no significant differences in the MDBT between the two groups with or without positive alleles of Qpc-sdau-3B.1 in all the trial populations (Table S4). The trait correlations probably mean pleiotropic or linked loci existed in the area. The intrinsic correlations between PC, ETN and GN could benefit the improvement of breeding efficiency for selecting multiple elite traits.

Our results showed that the PC was not correlated with the TKW which is inconsistent with the previous study. Zhao reported that the RILs carrying positive alleles of tiller angles QTL exhibited a 5.5% higher TKW (2.5 g) than those possessing contrasting pair of alleles, i.e., genotypes with smaller tiller angles had a higher TKW [40]. These results may be explained by the fact that we used a different mapping population and different field management practices.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, six QTL loci closely related to plant compactness in wheat were successfully identified through genetic analysis. Qpc.sdau-3B.1, which displays pleiotropic effects or is closely linked to traits affecting grain traits, enhances our understanding of the complex genetic interactions influencing wheat’s plant compactness. Although the individual effects of minor QTL are not significant, their interaction with the environment may elucidate the genetic basis of crop adaptability in plant architecture. Plant architecture plays a crucial role in enhancing yield and economic value in wheat. In the process of molecular marker-assisted selection breeding, the major QTL serves as the selection target, with attention given to the cumulative effect and environmental adaptability of the minor QTL. By optimizing light energy utilization, ventilation, and lodging resistance characteristics in wheat populations, it is possible to regulate and increase the effective number of spikes, grains per spike, and thousand grain weight. Through precise manipulation of the plant architecture control QTL, continuous optimization of wheat varieties can be promoted, leading to high-yield and efficient wheat production.
